lead: The halting problem asks one question about a Turing machine M and an input w: does M stop on w? Turing proved that no Turing machine can answer this for every pair (M,w). The proof uses self-reference: a machine is given its own code. The result limits compilers, static analyzers and program verifiers. A tool can run any program on a universal machine, but no general tool can always predict whether the program will stop.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for recursive and r.e. languages, 6.2 for decidable problems, and Unit 5 for the universal Turing machine.

sections.h3: The set HALT and its code

blocks.text: Let M be a Turing machine and w a string over its input alphabet. The pair ⟨M,w⟩ is a single string that codes both M and w. Some syllabi use a binary code over {0,1}; the exact code does not matter if a machine can read it and recover M and w.
HALT = { ⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on input w }
blocks.where: M is a Turing machine, w is an input string, and ⟨M,w⟩ is a computable code of the pair. HALT contains exactly the coded pairs for which M reaches a halting state.
M accepts w when M halts in an accepting state. A_TM is the acceptance problem; HALT is the stopping problem and ignores whether M accepts or rejects.

blocks.text: Both sets are undecidable. No Turing machine halts on every coded pair and answers yes or no correctly. HALT is the cleaner set for the diagonal proof because "halts" has only two outcomes, while "accepts" also has a rejecting halt.
Assume, for contradiction, that a Turing machine H decides HALT. H reads ⟨M,w⟩ and halts with yes if M halts on w, and no if M loops on w. H itself always halts.

items: Build a new Turing machine D. On input ⟨M⟩, D computes H(⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩). This asks whether M halts when M is run on its own code.
If H answers yes, D enters an infinite loop.
If H answers no, D halts.
Run D on its own code ⟨D⟩. D halts on ⟨D⟩ exactly when H says that D loops on ⟨D⟩. By the construction, that happens exactly when D loops on ⟨D⟩.
So D halts on ⟨D⟩ if and only if D loops on ⟨D⟩. Both cases contradict the assumed correctness of H.

blocks.text: The figure shows the same idea as a table. Rows are machines M1 to M4; columns are their codes. The marked diagonal asks each machine about its own code. D answers opposite to every marked cell, so D cannot be any row. Feeding D its own code puts D on the diagonal and forces the contradiction.

sections.h3: r.e., not recursive, and close variants

blocks.text: HALT is recursively enumerable. A universal Turing machine can simulate M on w step by step. If M halts, the simulation stops and the machine accepts ⟨M,w⟩. If M loops, the simulation runs forever. This is an acceptor, not a decider.

HALT is not recursive. A recursive language has a decider, and HALT has none. The complement of HALT is not r.e. If both HALT and its complement were r.e., interleaving the two acceptors would decide HALT: run both simulations in parallel and stop when one accepts. That would make HALT recursive, a contradiction.

items: Halting on empty input: HALT_ε = { ⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε } is undecidable. From M and w, build M_w that erases its input and simulates M on w. Then M_w halts on ε exactly when M halts on w.

Halting on every input: HALT_all = { ⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input } is undecidable. From M and w, build M' that on any input simulates M on w and then halts. M' halts on every input exactly when M halts on w.
Halting on own code: HALT_self = { ⟨M⟩ : M halts on ⟨M⟩ } is undecidable. The diagonal argument works directly: a decider for HALT_self lets D flip its own answer.

blocks.text: These variants are reductions from HALT. A decider for a variant would give a decider for HALT, which cannot exist.

A loop checker is a program that reads source code and always says whether the program terminates on a given input. If such a checker existed, it would decide HALT. So no general loop checker exists. The same limit hits full program verifiers: proving that a program always returns or never crashes on all inputs can encode termination.

The universal machine of Unit 5 can run any program. It cannot decide non-halting: after any finite number of steps, a running program may stop later. A practical tool can prove termination for restricted languages or find bugs, but it cannot be correct for every program and every input.
Rice's theorem in 6.4 generalizes the result to every nontrivial property of the language a machine accepts. The running time of the simulation is studied in 6.7.

figure.caption: Columns are the codes of M1 to M4, rows are the machines. The machine D answers opposite to each marked diagonal entry, so D behaves like no row in the table.

spec.title: Halting behaviour and the flipped diagonal
spec.aria: A four by four table of yes and no answers, with the main diagonal marked, showing where each machine is questioned about its own code.

examples.question: The four-machine table has rows M1: yes, no, yes, no; M2: no, no, yes, yes; M3: yes, yes, no, no; M4: no, yes, no, yes. The diagonal entries are yes, no, no, yes. Assume a decider H for HALT exists. Build D as in the proof, list D's four answers, and use D on its own code to derive a contradiction. State the number of machines, the number of diagonal cells D flips, and the number of yes on the diagonal.
steps: H(⟨M,w⟩) = yes when M halts on w, and no otherwise. H always halts.
Diagonal entries: H(⟨M1,⟨M1⟩⟩) = yes, H(⟨M2,⟨M2⟩⟩) = no, H(⟨M3,⟨M3⟩⟩) = no, H(⟨M4,⟨M4⟩⟩) = yes. The diagonal vector is yes, no, no, yes.
D on code ⟨Mi⟩ runs H(⟨Mi,⟨Mi⟩⟩). If H says yes, D loops; if H says no, D halts. So D's answer vector is the flip: no, yes, yes, no.
D differs from M1 at cell 0, from M2 at cell 1, from M3 at cell 2, and from M4 at cell 3. D differs from all 4 rows.
Feed D its own code. If H says D halts on ⟨D⟩, then D loops on ⟨D⟩. If H says D loops on ⟨D⟩, then D halts on ⟨D⟩. Both cases contradict H's correctness.
Therefore H cannot exist: HALT is undecidable. Counts: 4 machines, 4 diagonal cells flipped, 2 diagonal entries equal to yes.
examples.answer: HALT is undecidable; in this table D flips 4 diagonal cells, differs from all 4 rows, and the diagonal has 2 yes entries.

diag = [rows[i][i] for i in range(4)]

traps: Do not say "run M on w" decides HALT. A long run without a halt is not a no answer.
Keep H and D separate. H is the assumed decider for HALT; D is the machine built to contradict H.
HALT asks about stopping, A_TM asks about accepting. A machine can halt by rejecting, so the sets are different.
Recursive means a decider that always halts. Recursively enumerable allows looping on strings not in the language; HALT is r.e. but not recursive.
The diagonal table is not a practical algorithm. It is a proof by contradiction; the entries are assumed answers from H.

quiz.q: State HALT and say whether it is decidable.
quiz.a: HALT = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w}. It is undecidable.

quiz.q: Why does running M on w for more and more steps not decide HALT?
quiz.a: If M has not halted after t steps, it may halt later. No finite t proves that M loops. A decider must stop with no for every looping pair.

quiz.q: In the four-machine table, the diagonal is yes, no, no, yes. List D's four answers in order.
quiz.a: D flips each answer: no, yes, yes, no.

quiz.q: Explain why HALT is r.e. but not recursive.
quiz.a: A universal machine simulates M on w and accepts if M halts, so HALT is r.e. No decider exists by diagonalization, so HALT is not recursive.

quiz.q: Show that the complement of HALT is not r.e.
quiz.a: If both HALT and its complement were r.e., run their acceptors in parallel. One accepts every coded pair, giving a decider for HALT. HALT is not recursive, contradiction.

quiz.q: Reduce HALT to HALT_ε, the set of machines that halt on empty input.
quiz.a: Given M,w, build M_w that erases its input and simulates M on w. M_w halts on ε iff M halts on w. A decider for HALT_ε decides HALT.

quiz.q: Does the universal Turing machine contradict the halting problem? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The universal machine runs a given program. It does not decide in advance whether the program will halt. Running is not deciding non-halting.
Assume a decider for A_TM. Build D that on ⟨M⟩ accepts when the decider says M does not accept ⟨M⟩, and loops otherwise. D on ⟨D⟩ contradicts. So A_TM is undecidable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Termination analysis is an active area: tools try to prove that programs in restricted languages stop, and proof assistants check termination of functions. The busy beaver function grows faster than any computable function and is linked to the halting problem. Rice's theorem gives the general limit for program properties. Search next for "termination analysis", "busy beaver", and "Rice's theorem".
